transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I’m here because the clinic was kind of on me about how little I’ve been eating. I guess they made it sound like it was a bigger deal than I feel like it is, but I know it’s been… not much.

Most days I’m up early for the warehouse, and I’ll just grab coffee before I go in, because if I sit down and do breakfast it feels like it messes up my whole day before it even starts. Then after work, if I have GED class, I might have a yogurt or just a few bites of something, but not like a real meal. I know that sounds bad when I say it out loud, but in my head it’s like I’m just trying to keep everything in line and not feel thrown off.

So I guess that’s why I’m here. They wanted me to talk to someone about it.
Do you find yourself worrying about gaining weight or feeling like you need to keep your weight in check, even if others might say you're at a normal or low weight?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t always say it like that, like “I’m worried about gaining weight,” but yes, I guess that’s what it is.

Like if there’s fried food in the break room at work, or someone brings something in and I have some, even if it’s not a huge amount, I’ll start thinking about it after. Or at church, if there’s a big plate of food and I eat more than I meant to, it’s like I can feel myself getting nervous before I’m even done. I start thinking it’s going to show on me right away, like people will be able to tell, or my clothes will feel different, or the scale is going to be up.

And then I keep going over it in my head. Like, “Why did I eat that?” or “How much was that actually?” It’s hard to just let it go. I’ll want to check the scale, because otherwise I feel like I don’t know what’s happening with my body. So… yeah, I do feel like I have to keep it in check, even if other people don’t think it’s something I need to worry about.
Have you ever made yourself sick or used something like laxatives, diet pills, or enemas to control your weight after eating something you felt was too much?

Um… no, not like that. I mean, I’ve felt really bad after eating more than I planned, and I’ll get stuck thinking about it, but I haven’t made myself throw up or used laxatives or diet pills or enemas or anything like that.

I guess I’ve heard of people doing that, but that’s not really been my thing. For me it’s more like I just get anxious afterward and wish I hadn’t eaten it, but I don’t… do those things to get rid of it.
Do you ever push yourself to exercise more than you want to, or for longer than you planned, as a way to make up for eating something you felt was too much or too heavy?

I don’t really think so… not in the way you’re saying, like going to the gym for hours or making myself run because I ate something. I’m on my feet a lot at work already, packing and moving around, and sometimes I’ll feel better if I stay busy instead of just sitting with that heavy feeling after eating, but I wouldn’t say I have, like, an exercise routine I punish myself with.

I mean, I do think about it sometimes, like if I ate more than I meant to, I might think, “Well, at least I was moving around today,” or I’ll be relieved if I had a busy shift. But I don’t usually decide, “Okay, now I have to exercise for this long to make up for it.” It’s more just… I notice whether I’ve been active or not, and it can make me feel a little less panicky, I guess.

But no, I haven’t been pushing myself to exercise past what I wanted or anything like that. Mostly I just go to work and class and do what I have to do.
How much of a gap is there between what you would like to eat and what you actually allow yourself to eat, and has that gap changed over time?

It’s… it’s a pretty big gap, I guess. Bigger than I like admitting, because in my head I’ll think, like, “I should probably just eat something normal,” like a real breakfast or a plate of food after class, something that would actually count as a meal. And sometimes I even want that, not always in a craving way, but just because I’m tired and I know coffee isn’t really the same as food.

But then when it comes time to actually do it, I’ll pull back. Most days before the warehouse I just grab coffee, and then I tell myself I’ll eat later, like after my shift or after GED class. But then later comes and I’ll maybe have a yogurt, or a few bites of something, and then I stop because sitting down for a real meal feels like it messes everything up. Like once I start eating a full meal, I feel like I’ve lost control of what I was trying to keep in line.

And, yeah, that’s part of why I’m here. The clinic kind of got on me about how little I’ve been eating, and I didn’t think of it as that bad at first because I’m still going to work, I’m still getting through class, I’m still doing what I have to do. But when I say it out loud, it does sound like… not much.

It’s changed over time, I think. It used to be more like I’d skip something here or there, or just eat light if I felt like I needed to. Now it’s more like that has become the normal day. Coffee is easy. A yogurt is easy. A few bites is easy. A real meal feels like this whole thing I have to deal with afterward, so I just keep putting it off.
When you think about eating a full meal, does it feel more like you're not interested in food, or more like you're afraid of what eating it might mean for your body or how you look?

It’s more the second one, I think. Like, I wouldn’t say I’m just not interested in food. Sometimes food sounds good, or I’ll see something and part of me does want it. But then almost right away I start thinking about what it’s going to do, like… if I eat fried food from the break room, or if there’s a big plate at church and I actually eat all of it, I get this scared feeling that it’s going to show on me right away.

I know that probably sounds dramatic, because obviously one meal doesn’t instantly change everything, but in the moment it feels like it does. Like I can almost picture it on my body, or I feel like my clothes are going to fit different, and then I can’t stop thinking about it. I’ll want to check the scale, just to know, even though sometimes checking makes me feel worse too.

So it’s not really that I don’t care about eating. It’s more like eating a full meal feels risky, like I’m going to lose control and it’s going to show.
When you think about eating a full meal, do you ever feel like your body looks or will look a certain way, even if others might not see it that way?

Yeah… I think that happens a lot, honestly. Like, I can know in my head that someone else might not notice anything, or they might say I look fine, but when I’m looking at myself it doesn’t really feel that way.

Especially before class, or before softball if I’m changing or trying to figure out what to wear, I’ll look in the mirror and my stomach and my thighs just look… bigger than they should. I don’t even know what “should” means exactly, but it’s like my brain has this line, and if I look past that line then it ruins my whole mood. I’ll keep looking from different angles, pulling at my shirt, checking how my pants sit, and it starts feeling like that’s the truth of the day.

And it’s not just, “Oh, I don’t like this outfit.” It turns into, like, if my stomach looks flatter or my thighs don’t look as big, then I feel like I’m doing good, like I’ve been disciplined or something. But if they look bigger, even if nothing actually changed, then I feel like I failed already before the day even started. Then class feels harder because I’m sitting there aware of my body, or at softball I’m thinking about how I look moving around instead of just being there. So yeah… even if other people wouldn’t see it that way, I do.
How much does your concern about your weight or body shape interfere with your daily life, like at work, in class, or with friends?

It interferes… more than I want to admit, I think. I mean, I’m still showing up. I go to work, I get through my shifts packing, I go to GED class, so part of me keeps saying, “See, you’re fine, you’re doing what you’re supposed to do.” But it takes up so much space in my head while I’m doing those things.

Like at work, I’ll be thinking about when I last ate, what I’m going to allow myself later, whether I can keep the day on track. And if something changes, like someone offers food or plans get moved around, it throws me off more than it probably should. I get really stuck on keeping the eating and the schedule controlled, like if I don’t keep it tight then everything is going to get away from me.

With church, I’ve been turning down meals afterward more than I used to. People will invite me or there’ll be food, and I’ll make excuses, like I have something to do or I’m not hungry, but really it’s because eating there feels too unpredictable. I don’t know exactly what’s in the food or how much I’m supposed to have, and then I’ll be thinking about it the whole time instead of just being with people.

And class… I still go, but I’ve been leaving GED homework unfinished because I’ll spend so much time trying to organize my day around food and making sure I don’t mess up my routine. Or I sit down to do it and my mind keeps going back to what I ate or what I’m not going to eat, and then suddenly it’s late and I haven’t done what I needed to do. So it’s not like I’ve completely stopped my life, but it’s definitely getting in the way.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently, or do you feel like your weight is unusually low for your height and build?

Yeah… I mean, I guess people around me would say that. My work pants have gotten loose enough that I notice it when I’m moving around, like I have to keep adjusting them, and other people have made comments that I look too thin. Not just one person either, so I know it’s probably something they’re seeing.

But it’s hard because when I see the number go down, it doesn’t feel like a problem to me in that moment. It feels like I’m finally getting somewhere, like something is working and I’m doing it right. So when people say I should put weight back on, I get really uncomfortable and kind of defensive, because I don’t see why that should be the goal if I feel like I still need to keep going.

I know that probably sounds like I’m not answering the question straight, but… yes, I’ve lost enough that my clothes fit different and people are saying things. I just don’t really feel the same urgency about it that they seem to.
Do you feel like your eating habits are necessary to maintain a certain body shape or weight that you believe is important to who you are or how others see you?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t always say it like that in my head, like “this is important to who I am,” but it feels that way when I’m actually in it.

Like before class or before softball, if I look in the mirror and my stomach or my thighs look bigger than I think they should, it just changes everything. I’ll be standing there trying to get ready, and suddenly it’s not just about clothes or being on time. It feels like proof of whether I’m doing good or whether I’m failing. If I look flatter or smaller, I feel more okay, like I have control and I can handle being around people. But if I look bigger, even if maybe nobody else would notice, I feel embarrassed and distracted, like that’s what people are going to see when they look at me.

So I guess my eating habits feel necessary because I’m trying to keep from having that feeling. Like I’m trying to keep my body from crossing some line in my head. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but in the moment it really does feel like if I don’t keep controlling it, then I’ll look wrong, and then I’ll feel wrong for the whole day.
Do you feel like your value as a person, or how well you're doing in life, depends on your weight or body shape?

Yeah… I think it does, even though I don’t really like admitting that out loud. It’s like, logically I know my whole value as a person shouldn’t be about my body, but when I’m actually looking at myself, it doesn’t feel logical at all.

Like before class or before softball, I’ll check the mirror, and if my stomach or my thighs look bigger than I think they should, it can just… decide the whole day for me. I’ll feel like I’m already failing before I even leave the house. And it’s not just “I don’t like this outfit” or something normal like that. It feels deeper, like if I look that way then I’m not doing well, or I’m not disciplined enough, or people are going to see that I’ve messed up somehow.

And if I look smaller, or flatter, then I feel more okay. Like I’m doing good, like I can go out and be around people and not feel so ashamed or distracted. But if I look bigger in the mirror, even if maybe it’s just in my head, I carry that with me. I’ll be in class or at softball and still thinking about it, like it’s proof of how I’m doing as a person.

So… yeah. I don’t want it to be that way, but my weight and shape feel tied to whether I’m doing good or failing.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for work and class, but I’ve been turning down meals after church and leaving GED homework unfinished because I’m so focused on keeping my eating and schedule controlled.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how concerns about weight or body shape interfere with daily functioning at work, class, or socially, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
It interferes… more than I want to admit, I think. I mean, I’m still showing up. I go to work, I get through my shifts packing, I go to GED class, so part of me keeps saying, “See, you’re fine, you’re doing what you’re supposed to do.” But it takes up so much space in my head while I’m doing those things.

Like at work, I’ll be thinking about when I last ate, what I’m going to allow myself later, whether I can keep the day on track. And if something changes, like someone offers food or plans get moved around, it throws me off more than it probably should. I get really stuck on keeping the eating and the schedule controlled, like if I don’t keep it tight then everything is going to get away from me.

With church, I’ve been turning down meals afterward more than I used to. People will invite me or there’ll be food, and I’ll make excuses, like I have something to do or I’m not hungry, but really it’s because eating there feels too unpredictable. I don’t know exactly what’s in the food or how much I’m supposed to have, and then I’ll be thinking about it the whole time instead of just being with people.

And class… I still go, but I’ve been leaving GED homework unfinished because I’ll spend so much time trying to organize my day around food and making sure I don’t mess up my routine. Or I sit down to do it and my mind keeps going back to what I ate or what I’m not going to eat, and then suddenly it’s late and I haven’t done what I needed to do. So it’s not like I’ve completely stopped my life, but it’s definitely getting in the way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's weight is below normal for someone of their height and age, which would differentiate between F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa, non-subtype specified) and F50.01 (Anorexia Nervosa, restricting type).
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently, or do you feel like your weight is unusually low for your height and build?

target_item.name: Low_Weight
target_item.manifestation: Even with my work pants loose and people saying I look too thin, when I see the number go down I feel like I’m finally getting somewhere, and I don’t see why I should be pushed to put it back on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether my body weight is significantly low or whether I have lost a significant amount of weight recently.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I guess people around me would say that. My work pants have gotten loose enough that I notice it when I’m moving around, like I have to keep adjusting them, and other people have made comments that I look too thin. Not just one person either, so I know it’s probably something they’re seeing.

But it’s hard because when I see the number go down, it doesn’t feel like a problem to me in that moment. It feels like I’m finally getting somewhere, like something is working and I’m doing it right. So when people say I should put weight back on, I get really uncomfortable and kind of defensive, because I don’t see why that should be the goal if I feel like I still need to keep going.

I know that probably sounds like I’m not answering the question straight, but… yes, I’ve lost enough that my clothes fit different and people are saying things. I just don’t really feel the same urgency about it that they seem to.

inference.note: The patient meets criteria for anorexia nervosa (F50.00) with features that could include atypical anorexia (F50.01). No new disorders are added, and current information does not rule out either condition definitively.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restrictive eating behaviors are driven by a disturbance in the experience of body weight or shape, which is a key distinguishing feature of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) versus Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01).
doctor.question: Do you feel like your eating habits are necessary to maintain a certain body shape or weight that you believe is important to who you are or how others see you?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I look in the mirror before class or softball, my stomach and thighs still look bigger than they should, and it can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether eating habits are tied to maintaining a body shape or weight that feels important to identity or how others see the patient, which most directly reflects undue influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I don’t always say it like that in my head, like “this is important to who I am,” but it feels that way when I’m actually in it.

Like before class or before softball, if I look in the mirror and my stomach or my thighs look bigger than I think they should, it just changes everything. I’ll be standing there trying to get ready, and suddenly it’s not just about clothes or being on time. It feels like proof of whether I’m doing good or whether I’m failing. If I look flatter or smaller, I feel more okay, like I have control and I can handle being around people. But if I look bigger, even if maybe nobody else would notice, I feel embarrassed and distracted, like that’s what people are going to see when they look at me.

So I guess my eating habits feel necessary because I’m trying to keep from having that feeling. Like I’m trying to keep my body from crossing some line in my head. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but in the moment it really does feel like if I don’t keep controlling it, then I’ll look wrong, and then I’ll feel wrong for the whole day.

inference.note: The patient continues to meet criteria for both Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) and Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01). No additional information has ruled out either diagnosis. The patient restricts food intake, expresses significant fear of weight gain, experiences body image disturbance, and has lost weight, but does not engage in compensatory behaviors. The distinction between typical and atypical remains unclear based on current information.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's self-evaluation is unduly influenced by their body shape or weight, which is a key distinguishing feature of anorexia nervosa (F50.00) compared to anorexia not otherwise specified (F50.01).
doctor.question: Do you feel like your value as a person, or how well you're doing in life, depends on your weight or body shape?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I look in the mirror before class or softball, my stomach and thighs still look bigger than they should, and it can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether self-worth or sense of doing well depends on weight or body shape, which matches undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think it does, even though I don’t really like admitting that out loud. It’s like, logically I know my whole value as a person shouldn’t be about my body, but when I’m actually looking at myself, it doesn’t feel logical at all.

Like before class or before softball, I’ll check the mirror, and if my stomach or my thighs look bigger than I think they should, it can just… decide the whole day for me. I’ll feel like I’m already failing before I even leave the house. And it’s not just “I don’t like this outfit” or something normal like that. It feels deeper, like if I look that way then I’m not doing well, or I’m not disciplined enough, or people are going to see that I’ve messed up somehow.

And if I look smaller, or flatter, then I feel more okay. Like I’m doing good, like I can go out and be around people and not feel so ashamed or distracted. But if I look bigger in the mirror, even if maybe it’s just in my head, I carry that with me. I’ll be in class or at softball and still thinking about it, like it’s proof of how I’m doing as a person.

So… yeah. I don’t want it to be that way, but my weight and shape feel tied to whether I’m doing good or failing.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Anorexia Nervosa, Binge-Eating/Purging Type, based on restrictive eating behaviors, intense fear of gaining weight, body image disturbance, and significant weight loss confirmed by both patient report and external observation. There is no evidence of regular compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives, which rules out the Purging Type and supports the diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa, Binge-Eating/Purging Type.
